records.our_prose: Pick zucchini while it is still small, about 6 to 8 inches long, with shiny skin. Round kinds are best picked at about the size of a tennis ball. Zucchini grows surprisingly fast, so check your plants every day or two, it can go from small to oversized in just a couple of days. Cut the stem with a knife instead of pulling. If you leave squash on the plant too long it gets big, tough, and seedy, and the plant slows down. Picking often keeps more squash coming.
records.source_context: Harvesting In addition to describing the time of planting, "summer squash" refers to their short storage life, compared to winter squashes. Harvest immature fruits, about 6- to 8-inches long and 1½ to 2 inches in diameter for elongated types; 3 to 4 inches in diameter for pattypan types; and 4 to 7 inches long for yellow crooked neck.

records.our_prose: In the Southeast and Gulf, zucchini grows in two seasons: spring and fall, with a break in the hottest part of summer. Plant in spring once frost has passed, then plant again in late summer for a fall crop. Skip the peak of summer, when heat and pests make squash struggle. A spring sowing plus a second one a couple of weeks later gives you a good early supply.

records.our_prose: St. George's low-elevation Dixie belt (Mojave-edge high desert) runs zucchini on one spring cycle only, per USU Extension's Suggested Vegetable Planting Dates for Utah. Direct-sow around March 15, the Group C (Tender) date for St. George, about two weeks ahead of the March 30 average last frost; the table's explicit local date runs earlier than a generic frost-relative rule would. Harvest begins about 55 days later, around May 9, and continues into late June. Once St. George's daytime highs push past 95°F and the county's own frost-and-elevation data show summer highs routinely reaching 100°F in June through August, flowers and small fruit drop as pollen viability collapses. USU documents fall planting for cool-season crops in the St. George area but gives no fall or summer-replant window for zucchini, so there is no second cycle here; frost returns around November 1, well after the plants have already stopped producing for the year.

records.our_prose: Aim for about 1 inch of water per week, more in heat or sandy soil, delivered deeply and less often rather than in light daily sprinkles. Container plants dry out faster and often need water every day or two at peak.
records.source_context: If the soil becomes too dry, their growth may be seriously limited. Most vegetable crops require 1 inch of water per week for optimum pro- duction. If your area does not receive this amount of rainfall each week during the growing season, you will need to irrigate your garden using overhead sprinklers, soaker hoses, drip tape or hand watering.

records.our_prose: Water the soil, not the leaves. Use a soaker hose or aim a watering wand at the base of the plant. Keeping the leaves dry helps prevent powdery mildew, a common zucchini problem. A layer of mulch keeps the soil evenly moist.
